passage:
At nine, Sharmila had a shelf of puzzles she could do without thinking. When Chandrika Ma'am put a new logic puzzle on her desk, Sharmila slid it aside. "I'll get it wrong." She went back to a puzzle she already knew. She was safe, but the new one never got touched.
At fifteen, the science assignment was due on Monday and Sharmila had not started. On Sunday night her friend Mridul sent his finished answers. She stared at them. Her stomach clenched: if she wrote her own and it was wrong, what then? She told herself it was only this once, that many in class did it, and she copied most of it with a few words changed. On Monday, when Chandrika Ma'am asked her to explain question three, Sharmila's mouth went dry. She could not explain what she had written. Chandrika Ma'am asked her to stay after class, and spoke calmly. "I would rather see a wrong answer of your own than a right one that isn't yours. What made it hard to start?" Sharmila's eyes filled. "I was scared of getting it wrong." Chandrika Ma'am nodded. "Let's go through question three together, mistakes and all."

qa.q: On which day was the science assignment due?
How does Sharmila's avoidance at nine connect to her copying at fifteen?
qa.a: At nine she only did puzzles she knew because she feared being wrong. At fifteen the same fear of getting it wrong made copying feel like an easy way out, but she could not explain the answers, which showed the copying left her own understanding weaker.

qa.q: What was Sharmila feeling on Sunday night when her stomach clenched?
qa.a: She was anxious and afraid of failing, so copying seemed like a way to escape the risk of a wrong answer.

qa.q: What did Chandrika Ma'am do well when she saw the copied work?
qa.a: She stayed calm, asked what made it hard to start, and offered to work through question three together, so Sharmila could learn from mistakes.

grounding: A child who only does puzzles she can solve (4032) and, as a teen, copies out of fear of failure, which erodes her own ability (5190).
